```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4)
```

Bacterial isolates are not independent. Isolates from the same lineage share
most of their genome and, often, their resistance phenotype. A predictor can
look accurate simply because test isolates have close relatives in the
training data. This vignette uses simulated data, where the truth is known, to
show how AMRvalid exposes that.

```{r setup}
library(AMRvalid)
```

```{r palette, include = FALSE}
# Colourblind-safe pair used in all figures:
# orange = naive estimate, blue = population-aware estimate
col_naive <- "#eb6834"
col_aware <- "#2a78d6"
ink_muted <- "#6b6b6b"
grid_col <- "#e6e6e3"
```

## A simulated collection

`amr_simulate()` creates isolates in lineages. Resistance depends on a causal
marker and on a lineage effect that is inherited clonally but not explained by
the marker. Two fixed predictors are then applied:

* **knn** predicts from the 5 genomically nearest training isolates, so it
  memorises lineages;
* **marker** predicts from the marker alone, so it learns the mechanism.

Each is evaluated under a **random** split and a **lineage-held-out** split,
and on an **external** set of lineages never seen in training.

```{r simulate}
sim <- amr_simulate(n_lineages = 30, isolates_per_lineage = 15,
                    external_lineages = 30, seed = 2026)
x <- amr_import_predictions(sim$predictions)
x
```

## Step 1: check the split

Before trusting any number, check what the split actually separates.

```{r splits}
checks <- amr_validate_splits(x, train_manifest = sim$train_manifest, group = "lineage")
checks$consistent_designs
```

Both designs keep isolates apart, but only the lineage-held-out design keeps
lineages apart. Claiming lineage-level generalisation for the random split
fails:

```{r claim}
random_only <- x[x$model_id == "knn/random" & x$dataset_id == "internal", ]
amr_validate_splits(random_only, train_manifest = sim$train_manifest,
                    group = "lineage", claimed_design = "group")
```

## Step 2: internal versus external performance

The external lineages approximate what happens when the predictor meets new
strains.

```{r optimism}
e <- suppressMessages(amr_evaluate(x, validate = FALSE))
auc <- as.data.frame(e)[e$metric == "roc_auc", c("model_id", "dataset_id", "estimate")]
auc_wide <- reshape(auc, idvar = "model_id", timevar = "dataset_id", direction = "wide")
names(auc_wide) <- c("model", "external", "internal")
auc_wide$optimism <- auc_wide$internal - auc_wide$external
auc_wide[, c("model", "internal", "external", "optimism")]
```

```{r optimism-plot, echo = FALSE}
m <- t(as.matrix(auc_wide[, c("internal", "external")]))
colnames(m) <- auc_wide$model
barplot(m, beside = TRUE, ylim = c(0, 1.15), ylab = "ROC-AUC", yaxt = "n",
        legend.text = c("internal test set", "external unseen lineages"),
        args.legend = list(x = "top", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, horiz = TRUE),
        col = c(col_naive, col_aware), border = NA, las = 1, cex.names = 0.8)
axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, 0.2), las = 1, lwd = 0)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = ink_muted)
```

The memorising predictor looks good under a random split and collapses on new
lineages. The lineage-held-out split is less optimistic, though with only six
test lineages it is still noisy. The marker predictor is stable because it
learned the mechanism.

## Step 3: performance against distance to training

`amr_distance_eval()` makes the same point without needing an external
dataset: it asks how performance changes as test isolates become less similar
to anything in training.

```{r distance}
knn_random <- x[x$model_id == "knn/random", ]
knn_random$dataset_id <- "all test isolates"
# Isolates within a lineage are less than about 20 units apart in this simulation
d <- amr_distance_eval(knn_random, distances = sim$distances,
                       train_manifest = sim$train_manifest, bands = c(0, 20, 100, Inf))
table(d$nearest$band)
d$trend[, c("model_id", "model", "effect", "lower", "upper", "n")]
```

```{r distance-plot, echo = FALSE}
bb <- d$by_band[d$by_band$metric == "roc_auc", ]
plot(seq_len(nrow(bb)), bb$estimate, ylim = c(0, 1), xlim = c(0.6, nrow(bb) + 0.4), xaxt = "n",
     type = "n", xlab = "Distance to nearest training isolate", ylab = "ROC-AUC", las = 1, bty = "n")
abline(h = seq(0, 1, 0.2), col = grid_col)
lines(seq_len(nrow(bb)), bb$estimate, col = col_aware, lwd = 2)
arrows(seq_len(nrow(bb)), bb$lower, seq_len(nrow(bb)), bb$upper, angle = 90, code = 3, length = 0.05,
       col = col_aware, lwd = 2)
points(seq_len(nrow(bb)), bb$estimate, pch = 21, bg = col_aware, col = "white", cex = 1.8, lwd = 2)
axis(1, at = seq_len(nrow(bb)), cex.axis = 0.8,
     labels = c("same lineage\n(< 20)", "nearby lineage\n(20-100)", "distant\n(> 100)")[seq_len(nrow(bb))],
     padj = 0.5, lwd = 0)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = ink_muted)
```

A positive slope for the squared error means predictions get worse with
distance. Test isolates with a relative from the same lineage in training are
easy; isolates from other lineages are close to a coin toss.

## Step 4: intervals that respect clustering

Resampling single isolates treats related isolates as independent and gives
intervals that are too narrow. Resampling whole lineages does not. Here both
are applied to the marker predictor on the external set (30 lineages of 15
isolates).

```{r bootstrap}
ext <- x[x$model_id == "marker/lineage" & x$dataset_id == "external", ]
by_isolate <- as.data.frame(amr_bootstrap(ext, resample_by = "isolate_id", B = 300, seed = 1))
by_lineage <- as.data.frame(amr_bootstrap(ext, resample_by = "lineage", B = 300, seed = 1))
ci <- rbind(
  isolate = unlist(by_isolate[by_isolate$metric == "roc_auc", c("estimate", "lower", "upper")]),
  lineage = unlist(by_lineage[by_lineage$metric == "roc_auc", c("estimate", "lower", "upper")])
)
cbind(ci, width = ci[, "upper"] - ci[, "lower"])
```

The lineage interval is substantially wider because 450 isolates carry the
information of only 30 independent lineages. The isolate-level interval
overstates precision.

## Take-aways

1. Check the split with `amr_validate_splits()` before reporting performance.
2. Prefer lineage- or cluster-held-out designs, or external datasets, when the
   claim is about new strains.
3. Use `amr_distance_eval()` to show how performance depends on similarity to
   the training data.
4. Use `amr_bootstrap()` with `resample_by = "lineage"` (or genomic clusters) so the
   uncertainty reflects the number of independent lineages, not isolates.
